title: AI Agents and Agent Architecture
description: Design agents you can trust: the loop, tools and protocols, memory, patterns for planning and composition, and the controls for permissions, injection, traces, evaluation and oversight.
audience: A developer who has called a language model from code. ai-engineering (tokens, prompts, retrieval, evaluation) is the recommended earlier course. Coding assistants are covered separately in ai-assisted-engineering.
outcomes: You'll be able to choose between a workflow, a copilot and an agent for a task.
You'll be able to trace an agent loop and compute its cost and reliability.
You'll be able to design tools and a server-side permission model.
You'll be able to recognise prompt injection and break the lethal trifecta.
You'll be able to instrument and evaluate an agent and stage its rollout.

lessons.title: Workflow, copilot or agent
lessons.objective: Place a process on the autonomy ladder and choose the lowest rung that meets the need.

concepts.title: Workflow
concepts.summary: Model calls and tools orchestrated by code along predefined paths.

concepts.title: Agent
concepts.summary: A system in which the model decides its own next steps and tool use within a loop.

concepts.title: Autonomy ladder
concepts.summary: Script, model-assisted workflow, copilot, agent: more freedom, less predictability.

misconceptions: Every AI feature should be an agent; extra autonomy buys flexibility at the cost of predictability, cost and auditability.
A chatbot with tools is automatically an agent; if the code fixes the path, it is a workflow.
sequence: One business process: classify and answer a refund request.

lessons.title: The agent loop
lessons.objective: Trace an agent loop step by step, add a stop condition and a step budget, and compute how errors compound.

concepts.title: Agent loop
concepts.summary: Repeat: model sees context, picks an action, the result is appended, until a stop condition holds.

concepts.title: Step budget
concepts.summary: A hard limit on iterations, tokens or time.

concepts.title: Compounding error
concepts.summary: Per-step reliability multiplies across steps.

misconceptions: The agent stops when it is done; without a limit it loops until the budget runs out.
Context stays constant; each step appends actions and results, so input tokens grow.
If every step is 95% reliable the task is 95% reliable; ten steps give about 60%.
sequence: Pseudocode of the loop.
One run traced: goal, step, tool call, observation.
Termination: final answer, budget, error, human stop.
Context growth and reliability arithmetic.
examples: Base context 1,000 tokens, +400 per step: input over 6 steps is 1,000, 1,400, 1,800, 2,200, 2,600, 3,000 = 12,000.

lessons.title: Designing tools
lessons.objective: Classify tools as read or write, write a tool description the model can use, and make a write tool safe to retry.

concepts.title: Tool description
concepts.summary: The name, purpose, parameters and limits that the model reads when choosing a tool.

concepts.title: Read versus write tool
concepts.summary: A read tool only fetches; a write tool changes state.

concepts.title: Idempotency key
concepts.summary: A caller-supplied token so a repeated request has the effect of one.

misconceptions: The model picks the right tool from its name alone; descriptions and error messages are prompts.
A retried write is harmless; a duplicate charge is a real harm.
sequence: Five tools for a support agent.
What a good description says: when to use it, inputs, what comes back, when not to use it.
Error messages that help the next step.
Idempotency on writes.
examples: search_orders and get_customer are reads; issue_refund and send_email are writes.

lessons.title: Tool protocols: MCP and agent-to-agent
lessons.objective: Read a JSON-RPC tool request and say which side owns each part of the Model Context Protocol.

concepts.title: Model Context Protocol
concepts.summary: An open protocol by which a client application discovers and calls tools, resources and prompts on a server.

concepts.title: JSON-RPC
concepts.summary: A message format of method, parameters and id, with a matching result or error.

concepts.title: Transport
concepts.summary: The channel carrying messages: standard input/output for local servers, HTTP for remote ones.

misconceptions: MCP is a framework for building agents; it is a wire protocol between hosts and tool servers.
The server decides which tool the model uses; the host and model do, and the server only describes and executes.
MCP and agent-to-agent protocols solve the same problem; one connects an agent to tools and data, the other agents to agents.
sequence: The integration problem: N applications times M tools.
Host, client and server roles.
Initialise, list tools, call a tool.
A tools/call message and its result.
examples: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"search_orders","arguments":{"customer":"c-42"}}}
Connecting 4 hosts to 6 tools needs 24 bespoke integrations, but 4 + 6 = 10 protocol implementations.

lessons.title: Memory and context management
lessons.objective: Decide what an agent keeps in context, summarises or stores outside it, and compute when compaction triggers.

concepts.title: Working context
concepts.summary: What is in the prompt on this step.

concepts.title: Compaction
concepts.summary: Summarising old turns to free room.

concepts.title: External memory
concepts.summary: Notes and files the agent writes and reads back by tool.

misconceptions: A bigger window removes the need for memory design; long contexts cost more and can be used less well.
Memory is retrieval; memory has writes, and a wrong write persists.
Summaries are lossless; they drop detail, which may be the detail needed later.
sequence: The window as a budget.
Three tiers: context, summary, external store.
What to write down: decisions, user preferences, open tasks.
When to compact.

lessons.title: Planning and reasoning patterns
lessons.objective: Choose between acting step by step, planning first and reflecting, given a task's predictability and cost of error.

concepts.title: Reason-act loop
concepts.summary: Interleave a short reasoning step with an action and an observation.

concepts.title: Plan then execute
concepts.summary: Write the whole plan first, then carry out steps, replanning on failure.

concepts.title: Reflection
concepts.summary: Critique the result or failure and retry with the critique.

misconceptions: Showing reasoning to the user is evidence the answer is right; it is not a verified account of the model's computation.
Planning first is always cheaper; a rigid plan fails when early observations change the task.
Reflection fixes errors; it needs a signal such as a test or a checker to be better than guessing.
sequence: A task with unknown steps: investigate a failing job.
A task with known steps: fill a form.
Plan, step, observe, replan.
Reflection with an external signal.
examples: A 6-step plan in which step 4 fails: replan from step 4, so 3 steps done, 1 failed, then a new 3-step tail: 7 actions in total.
A test result is a reliable reflection signal; the model's own opinion of its answer is not.

lessons.title: Composed workflow patterns
lessons.objective: Match a task to prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation, orchestrator-workers or evaluator-optimiser, and compute the latency and accuracy effects.

concepts.title: Prompt chaining
concepts.summary: A fixed sequence of model calls, each taking the previous output.

concepts.title: Parallelisation
concepts.summary: Independent subtasks run at once (sectioning) or the same task run several times (voting).

concepts.title: Evaluator-optimiser
concepts.summary: One call proposes, another critiques, and the loop repeats until accepted.

misconceptions: Parallel branches add their times; latency is the slowest branch.
Majority voting always improves accuracy; the votes must be independent and better than chance.
An orchestrator is just a bigger prompt; it decides subtasks at run time, which a fixed workflow cannot.
sequence: Five patterns and the task shape each fits.
Three branches taking 4, 6 and 5 s.
Voting with three 80% voters.
Where a pattern stops being a workflow and becomes an agent.
examples: Sequential 4 + 6 + 5 = 15 s, parallel max = 6 s.
Three independent 80% voters: P(majority right) = 3·0.8²·0.2 + 0.8³ = 0.384 + 0.512 = 0.896.

lessons.title: Multiple agents
lessons.objective: Say when splitting work between agents helps, count the token cost, and define the contract between agents.

concepts.title: Handoff
concepts.summary: One agent passing control and context to another.

concepts.title: Context isolation
concepts.summary: Giving a subagent only the context its task needs.

concepts.title: Agent contract
concepts.summary: The defined inputs, outputs and permissions between two agents.

misconceptions: More agents means more intelligence; each added agent adds tokens, latency and an interface that can fail.
A subagent sees everything the lead agent sees; it only sees what it is handed.
Agents can share state through chat; shared mutable state needs an owner.
sequence: A research task with four independent searches.
What a subagent buys: parallel time, a clean context.
What it costs: tokens multiplied, summaries lose detail, coordination bugs.
The contract: input spec, output schema, tool allow-list, budget.
examples: Lead plans in 10k tokens, four workers use 20k each = 80k, synthesis 10k: total 100k compared with perhaps 35k for one agent doing the task serially.

lessons.title: Permissions and governed actions
lessons.objective: Design the permission model for an agent's tools: scoped identity, approval for risky writes, audit log, budgets and a kill switch.

concepts.title: Least privilege
concepts.summary: Giving an agent only the access its task needs.

concepts.title: Approval gate
concepts.summary: A human decision required before a risky action runs.

concepts.title: Audit log
concepts.summary: An append-only record of each action with who, what and why.

misconceptions: The system prompt can enforce permissions; the server must check them, since a prompt can be bypassed.
Approving every action is the safest design; too many prompts train people to click yes.
An agent should reuse the user's full credentials; it needs its own scoped identity.
sequence: A support agent with read and write tools.
Tier the actions: read, reversible write, irreversible or costly write.
Server-side enforcement of each tier.
Audit, rate and spend limits, and an emergency disable.
examples: 1,000 approvals a day at 5 seconds each is 5,000 s, about 83 minutes of pure clicking.
Refunds under $20 auto-approve with logging; refunds over $20 need approval; account deletion is never available to the agent.

lessons.title: Prompt injection and the lethal trifecta
lessons.objective: Identify which of three dangerous capabilities an agent combines, and remove one.

concepts.title: Lethal trifecta
concepts.summary: Access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and a way to communicate externally, in one agent.

concepts.title: Untrusted content
concepts.summary: Any text the agent reads that an attacker could have written.

concepts.title: Privilege separation
concepts.summary: Splitting work so that the part reading untrusted content has no powerful tools.

misconceptions: Filtering for the word 'ignore' blocks injection; attackers rephrase and hide text in documents.
Only chat input is untrusted; web pages, emails, tool results and retrieved documents all are.
Human approval alone fixes it; a hurried approver misses the hidden action.
sequence: An email agent reads the inbox and can send mail.
The three legs.
Data exfiltration through a link or an outbound call.
Controls: remove a leg, split privileges, restrict outbound, approve outbound.
examples: An agent reading emails (private data + untrusted content) and with no way to send anything outside has two legs, so it cannot exfiltrate; adding a send_email tool adds the third.
A browser agent with a logged-in session has private data; browsing adds untrusted content; clicking links is outbound: all three.

lessons.title: Observability and traces
lessons.objective: Read an agent trace, compute p95 latency and cost per success, and decide what to redact.

concepts.title: Trace
concepts.summary: The record of one run as nested spans for model calls, retrievals and tool calls.

concepts.title: 95th percentile
concepts.summary: The value below which 95% of observations fall (nearest rank: the ceil(0.95·n)th smallest).

concepts.title: Cost per success
concepts.summary: Total spend divided by the number of successful tasks.

misconceptions: Averages describe latency; a few slow runs hide in the mean.
Log everything; traces hold personal data and secrets and need redaction and retention rules.
Cost per run is the cost metric; failed runs cost the same and deliver nothing.
sequence: One run as a tree of spans.
What each span records: input summary, output summary, duration, tokens, error.
Percentiles and rates.
Redaction before storage.
examples: Twenty sorted latencies end 3.4, 4.8, 9.5: the nearest-rank 95th is the 19th value, 4.8 s.

lessons.title: Evaluating agents
lessons.objective: Grade outcomes and trajectories, and compute pass@k against pass^k to describe reliability.

concepts.title: Trajectory
concepts.summary: The sequence of actions an agent took, not only its final answer.

concepts.title: pass@k
concepts.summary: The chance that at least one of k attempts succeeds.

concepts.title: pass^k
concepts.summary: The chance that all k attempts succeed.

misconceptions: The final answer is all that matters; a right answer reached by deleting records is a failure.
A 90% success agent is reliable; if the task repeats daily for a month, it will fail around three times.
Same prompt, same result; sampling and tool variance make repeated trials necessary.
sequence: A run with a correct answer and a forbidden action.
Outcome check (state of the environment) and trajectory check (allowed tools, step count).
k trials per task.
Regression gate on a critical suite.
examples: Per-trial success 0.8: pass@3 = 1 − 0.2³ = 0.992; pass^3 = 0.8³ = 0.512.

lessons.title: Human oversight, rollout and risk
lessons.objective: Place human control points, stage a rollout and map agent risk work onto the NIST AI RMF functions.

concepts.title: Oversight point
concepts.summary: Where a person approves, samples or can stop the agent.

concepts.title: Staged rollout
concepts.summary: Shadow, assist, then act, each gated by evidence.

concepts.title: Autonomy decision record
concepts.summary: A written decision stating the autonomy level, why, and the trigger for changing it.

misconceptions: A human in the loop is always safer; a person rubber-stamping at speed adds latency without checking.
Oversight ends at launch; monitoring and incident response continue.
Risk work belongs to the model team alone; govern, map, measure and manage involve owners, product and security.
sequence: Three oversight styles: approve first, review a sample after, alert on anomalies.
Shadow mode: the agent proposes, nothing executes.
Promotion gates from evaluation results.
An incident: how to stop the agent.
examples: Review 2% of 1,500 daily actions: 30 actions a day.
NIST AI RMF functions: Govern (policies, roles), Map (context, risks), Measure (evaluate), Manage (respond, improve).
